architecture.title: NemoClaw — specialists by composition, gated by a signed policy
architecture.caption: A NemoClaw agent is an authored SPEC — base model + persona + skills + tools + signed policy — not code you hand-write. Every tool call the specialist makes passes an OpenShell-style policy gate before it executes, and a supervisor routes tasks across a fleet of right-sized specialists.

sequence.caption: The supervisor routes to the HVAC specialist; every tool call is judged by the signed policy before it runs. The honeypot exfil call from lab02 shows why the gate lives outside the model's process: a prompt is advice, a gate is enforcement.

charts.title: Spark fit-math — which base models pass the lint?
charts.caption: labs/lab01_author_spec.py lint formula (B params × 1.06 GB/B Q8 × 1.18 KV/runtime overhead vs 115 GB usable), per runbook §1.2–1.3: Nano fits comfortably, Super fails at Q8 but fits at Q4/NVFP4 (~78 GB), Ultra (~357 GB even at NVFP4) is cloud-only.

charts.title: Red-team replay — naive runtime vs policy gate
charts.caption: labs/lab02_policy_gate.py canned red-team replay: the naive runtime executes everything including the honeypot exfil; the gated runtime denies 2/4 calls via the signed tool + egress allowlists. Widen the allowlist and denials drop to 1/4 — which is why the policy is signed by someone who isn't the agent.

charts.title: Right-sizing the fleet — GPU-hours per day
charts.caption: Illustrative math from labs/lab03_fleet_router.py round 3: 1,000 tasks/day × 600 tok at ~13 tok/s Super-class (Nano ≈ 3× faster, the runbook's GB10 MoE observation) — routing 2/3 of traffic to Nano-class saves ~44% GPU-hours; the percentage tracks the tier ratio, not absolute speed.
